A content delivery network, or CDN, is a system of computers spread across many cities that stores copies of websites and videos so people nearby can load them quickly. Every website normally lives on one main computer, called an origin server, which holds the real, original copy of everything. Without help, everyone in the world would have to fetch data from that single distant machine, which gets slow as distance and traffic increase. A CDN solves this by placing extra copies at an edge location, a smaller computer positioned closer to a particular city or region. When someone requests a page, the network checks whether the nearby edge location already has a saved copy; finding one there is called a cache hit, and it means the request never has to travel all the way back to the origin server. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books in stock, so readers do not need to travel to one central archive every time. This setup reduces waiting time, lowers the load on the origin server, and keeps things working even during busy periods.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The main computer holding the original, complete copy of a website | Everything ultimately comes from here if no closer copy exists |
| Edge location | A smaller computer placed closer to visitors, holding saved copies | Shortens the distance data must travel, speeding things up |
| Cache hit | A successful find of the needed copy at a nearby edge location | Avoids a slow trip to the distant origin server |
| Latency | The delay between asking for something and receiving it | Lower delay makes browsing feel instant rather than sluggish |
